title: MB5-04183
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection by determining that he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and of Rwanda. He is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection by determining that he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The appellant did not submit any new evidence in support of his appeal. He did not ask to be heard before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).1

He is requesting that the RAD allow the appeal and render a favourable decision. In the alternative, he is requesting that the RAD to refer the matter to the RPD for redetermination of his refugee protection claim by another panel.
The Minister did not intervene in the appeal.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.
In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the refugee protection claimant alleges the following.
He is a XXXX Tutsi born in the DRC. He went to live in Rwanda to complete his education. In 2008, he obtained Rwandan citizenship and found a job in the XXXX XXXX XXXX under the XXXX XXXX XXXX.
In 2009, the XXXX of the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) and a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX asked him to become an informant. He allegedly acted as though he accepted, but he left his job.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, he began working for the XXXX XXXX XXXX and also acted as a XXXX for XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The claimant alleged that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, members of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX arrested, detained and tortured him for three days to obtain information about a plot by XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX soldiers from the DRC.

On XXXX XXXX, 2013, on his way back from the DRC, he was held and interrogated at the border by Rwandan authorities about his alleged ties to XXXX XXXX. The claimant alleged that, in the months that followed, he was threatened with reprisals on several occasions.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, he allegedly changed jobs, hoping to avoid problems.

He alleged that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, when he was out for a walk, he was attacked and savagely beaten. He was saved by the shouts of passersby. On his release from hospital, he asked the police to investigate the incident, but nothing was done.
He left Rwanda on XXXX XXXX, 2015. He came to Canada and claimed refugee protection a few weeks later. Impugned decision

On September 9, 2015, the RPD rejected his refugee protection claim, stating that [translation] "the claimant's credibility was the determinative issue" because of significant omissions, contradictions, inconsistencies and implausibilities. The RPD noted the following: - First, the RPD considered that [translation] "his allegations clearly contradicted the claimant's remarkable and long career of many years in the XXXX XXXX XXXX". On this topic, the RPD found it implausible that a government which does not hesitate to eliminate its opponents would go as far as to offer training abroad to someone suspected of possessing information about a plot to overthrow the current regime; - The RPD drew an inference from the omission in the initial BOC Form of a threat to his life by assailants during the alleged attack on XXXX XXXX, 2015; - The RPD granted no probative value to the medical report filed as Exhibit P-13 to corroborate the incident. The RPD noted that the physician's signature is illegible, the medical certificate is undated, and it does not mention the date on which the claimant was allegedly seen at the medical clinical. In short, it only reports the claimant's words; - The claimant failed to inform the RPD in a timely manner that his wife had left Rwanda to seek refuge in Kenya as she no longer felt comfortable because she was receiving calls from a local authority who was looking for the claimant; - The RPD drew a negative inference from the fact that the claimant omitted to include in his BOC Form that he had been forced to make financial contributions to the party in power for many years; - The RPD found it implausible that the claimant was able to leave his country without any difficulties while the authorities are allegedly looking for him and even want to kill him because he is suspected of having links to XXXX XXXX; - The RPD found it inconsistent that his parents, brothers and sisters are still in Rwanda and do not have any problems with the current regime; - The RPD found that the alleged risk to his life is inconsistent with the fact that the claimant never hid, moved or changed his telephone number; - The RPD drew a negative inference from the fact that the claimant stayed in Kenya for three months in 2012 and returned to his country, while he alleged that he was tortured in a cell in Rwanda; - The RPD believed that his ethnic origin is Banyamulenge, but this element alone was not sufficient to conclude that he would face a serious possibility of persecution should he return to Rwanda. GROUNDS OF APPEAL AND REMEDY SOUGHT Appellant's arguments

With regard to his position in the Rwandan government, the appellant submits that the panel erred. According to him, RPD is not an organization that is [translation] "an expert on the Rwandan public service". The RPD [translation] "needed to rely on evidence indicating that the claimant's testimony did not correspond to the reality in Rwanda".2

Concerning the omission in the BOC Form that his assailants had threatened to kill him in the attack of XXXX XXXX, 2015, he argues that the conclusion is [translation] "clearly exaggerated and defies all logic". It is human nature to forget, and the fact that a person is educated and represented by counsel does not change the fact that the RPD made an error by drawing a negative inference regarding the omission in the initial BOC Form of the threats made by his assailants.

The appellant also submits that the RPD erred by not granting any probative value to the medical report. Counsel argues that the elements retained by the RPD, more specifically the fact that the physician's signature is illegible, [translation] "is the most far-fetched thing that the undersigned has read in quite a long time in an RPD determination. Frankly, this conclusion speaks for itself". Similarly, the fact that the physician reports the patient's statements about the circumstances in which he was injured, is [translation] "self-evident"; the physician was not there to be able to determine whether or not his patient was telling the truth.3 With regard to the fact that it was undated or that the date of the visit to the doctor was not indicated does not mean that the document has no probative value.

The panel also erred and its findings were unreasonable when it drew a negative inference from the fact that he failed to discuss his wife on his BOC Form. Moreover, he also did not indicate that he had contributed to the RPF (Rwandan Patriotic Front) when he worked for the XXXX XXXX XXXX4 RAD'S ROLE AND FUNCTIONS

The appellant filed submissions about the standard that the RAD must apply when it reviews a RPD decision. In summary, he submits that the RAD must proceed de novo, carry out its own assessment of the evidence and draw its own conclusions. It owes no deference to the RPD even when it is a matter of credibility findings.

In Huruglica,5 the Federal Court of Appeal ruled on the issue of whether it was reasonable for the RAD, where credibility is not at issue, to examine findings of fact or of mixed fact and law using the standard of reasonableness.

Interpreting the statutory provisions and noting in passing Parliament's intent when implementing the RAD, Justice Gauthier notes: [98] The RAD was essentially viewed as the safety net that would catch all mistakes made by the RPD, be it on the law or the facts.

The intent of Parliament must be determined by referring first to the wording used in the legislation, specifically in sections 110 and 111 of the IRPA. The Court of Appeal states as follows: [59] ... Paragraph 111(2)(a) does not distinguish between errors of law, fact or mixed fact and law. It simply requires that the decision of the RPD be "wrong in law, in fact or in mixed fact and law." [64] The ordinary meaning of the word "wrong" is "not correct or true", "incorrect", "mistaken:" The Oxford English Dictionary, 3d ed., s.v. "wrong." The French version "erronée" has the exact same ordinary meaning, that is, "fausse", "incorrecte", "inexacte", "mal fondée:" Le Nouveau Petit Robert, 2006, s.v. "erroné." This wording definitively points to the standard of correctness. In addition, the legislator's intent to use the word "wrong" in its ordinary meaning is, in my view, supported by the legislative history, to which I will refer later.

After noting some scenarios that may arise, the Court of Appeal mentions that the level of deference "owed in each case" varies, and concludes: [78] ... [T]he role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in fact and law. This translates into an application of the correctness standard of review. If there is an error, the RAD can still confirm the decision of the RPD on another basis. It can also set it aside, substituting its own determination of the claim, unless it is satisfied that it cannot do either without hearing the evidence presented to the RPD: paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA.

In answer to the Court of Appeal's question, Justice Gauthier stated the following: [103] ... [W]ith respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination.

Taking into account the decision, I will conduct an independent assessment of the evidence in order to formulate my own opinion on this refugee protection claim and to determine whether the decision is correct. If an error of fact, of law or of mixed law and fact was made, I will intervene using one of the remedies set out in sections 110 and 111 of the IRPA.
The RPD was of the opinion that the claimant did not establish that he is a credible and trustworthy witness with respect to the central elements in his claim.

In Huruglica,6 the Federal Court of Appeal acknowledges that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys an advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because they require assessment of the weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. As the degree of restraint "ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis," the RAD must determine whether, in light of the evidence, it can make a final decision or must send the matter to the RPD.

The claimant's negative credibility finding is based on several elements. Even if I am of the opinion that one of them may be wrong, I find that the decision rendered is the appropriate one in the circumstances. Here is why. Profile of the claimant

The RPD is of the opinion that the claimant's allegations [translation] "clearly contradicted the claimant's remarkable and long career of many years" in the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RPD considers that it is implausible and not credible that an individual who has opinions that are contrary to the regime, who was allegedly tortured because of his links to XXXX XXXX and who is suspected of wanting to overturn the existing regime, would be sent to Kenya for training.

The appellant argued that the RPD erred by reaching this conclusion and that it [translation] "needed evidence on which it could rely indicating that the claimant's testimony did not correspond to the reality in Rwanda.7 He argued that the RPD may believe that his situation is unusual, [translation] "but it is not impossible. There are many cases of persons who have opinions contrary to those of their supervisors holding a position in a given institution".8

With all due respect for the submissions, I share the opinion of the RPD. Of course, caution must be exercised when making an unfavourable conclusion based on the implausibility of a situation. However, it appears to me that the RPD was correct in this case. The assessment of credibility should take into account the social and political context in Rwanda, a regime controlled by the RPF, which "tightly controls political space, civil society and the media"9 and a country where any dissent is severely punished.

As stated by the Federal Court of Appeal in Aguebor,10 [translation] The panel is not under any obligation to accept testimony simply because it was not contradicted. It can base its decision on reason, common sense and rationality.
In this case, the alleged situation considered as a whole and in its context is implausible and even not credible.

The appellant submitted that he had been held in a cell and tortured in 2010 so that he would supply information about an alleged plot planned by XXXX XXXX to overthrow the government. The XXXX was in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX following a conflict with the current government. In my opinion, there are reasons to believe that this would be a matter of utmost importance for the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Consequently, it would be illogical for the XXXX in place that suspects the claimant of having ties with the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, to offer him training abroad, allowing him to advance his career. Return to Rwanda after being tortured
In the same vein, the appellant's return to Rwanda after three months of training in Kenya contradicts the credibility of his allegations that his life was at risk in Rwanda.

When questioned about it, the appellant testified at the hearing that he tried to leave the country, but he was unable to obtain a scholarship allowing him to study in Holland.11 The documents in the RPD file confirm that the appellant was admitted to the XXXX School of XXXX in XXXX 2010.12

The appellant claims that he was tortured in XXXX 2010 by reason of imputed political opinion, the same reason he fears returning to Rwanda today. Based on various decisions of the Federal Court,13 I would add that under section 96 of the IRPA, the appellant has not established his subjective fear of persecution by reason of [translation] "real or perceived political opinion." On this topic, I note the comments made by Justice Tremblay-Lamer in Kamana14 to the effect that: The lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim is a fatal flaw which in and of itself warrants dismissal of the claim, since both elements of the refugee definition-subjective and objective-must be met.

It is also my opinion because of this return to Rwanda, his allegations that his life is at risk under section 97 of the IRPA for the alleged reasons are not credible. It also casts serious doubt on his detention in XXXX 2010. Taking into account the alleged risk and the fact that his wife allegedly sought refuge in Kenya, the RPD was correct to dismiss his explanations that Kenya is part of the XXXX XXXX region to justify his return to Rwanda.15 Moreover, someone who fears for his or her life does not wait to receive a scholarship before leaving the country. Since he travelled abroad to Kenya, and this was not his only trip outside the country (he testified that he travelled to Burundi after the incident in XXXX 2013),16 I am of the opinion that the appellant, who claims to have been tortured, could have taken the opportunity to flee elsewhere if Kenya was not a safe country. Omission in the BOC Form

The RPD identified several omissions on the BOC Form. Specifically, it noted that the claimant failed to indicate that his life was threatened in the attack on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, that his wife left Rwanda because she did not feel safe, and that he was forced to make contributions to the RPF (the party in power).
In my opinion, the determinative omissions were the threats to his life and the fact that his spouse left Rwanda as she did not feel safe because a local authority was asking about her husband.

The appellant alleged that he received death threats when he was allegedly attacked in XXXX 2015. These death threats were not mentioned in the initial BOC Form. Considering the significance of this fact, the RPD draws a negative inference, even though the appellant added it to his amended BOC Form.

The appellant submits [translation] "the implication that he intended to lie to the panel because of the fact that he did not include the words said to him at the time of the attack on XXXX XXXX, 2015, is clearly exaggerated and defies all logic." Apparently, it was an oversight on his part.

The RPD may consider the omission of important facts in the BOC Form. In my opinion, the fact that he did not indicate in his BOC Form the words of his alleged assailants is one thing, but completely omitting that he was threatened with death is another. It is well established that the panel is entitled to consider the contents of the Personal Information Form (PIF) before and after it has been amended, and the panel may also draw negative conclusions about the claimant's credibility when matters considered important are included in the PIF by amendment at the hearing.17 In my opinion, death threats are not insignificant. The RPD was justified in drawing a negative inference from this omission on the initial BOC Form. Omission that his spouse left Rwanda

The RPD also drew a negative inference from the fact that the appellant did not mention in the BOC Form or the amended BOC Form that his wife had left the country as she no longer felt safe because of him.

At the hearing, the appellant testified that the XXXX XXXX XXXX had asked his wife about him. The claimant did not mention this fact in his BOC Form, which he amended twice.18 The RPD may consider the omission of this element from the amended BOC Form. Medical certificate

With regard to this document, I do not share the RPD's opinion when it determines that the document has no probative value because the physician's signature is illegible and it is undated, among other things. In my opinion, the RPD should have questioned the claimant to find out in which circumstances and for what reasons the certificate was issued. Having said that, I am of the opinion that this certificate alone is insufficient to establish that the claimant was attacked for the alleged reasons or that CID officers were at the origin of the attack.

The RPD drew a negative inference from the fact that the claimant continued to live at the same address until he left the country in 2015, when he alleged that the authorities had been looking for him since XXXX 2010.

In Ramirez,19 Justice Shore states that the IRB may take into account a claimant's conduct in the face of alleged risk. If he seriously feared persecution or his life was at risk, he would have moved or changed jobs at the first opportunity.

Even though the claimant indicated that he changed jobs in XXXX 2014 to get away from his problems, a review of his curriculum vitae compared with the information on Form IMM-5669 shows that he worked for the XXXX XXXX Company from XXXX 2013 until he left the country in XXXX 2015,20 whereas the information in his curriculum vitae indicates that he had worked as a "XXXX XXXX in XXXX XXXX XXXX." since XXXX 2012 and, at the time of preparing his curriculum vitae , which seemed to be in XXXX 2015, and he was still working there.21

In this context, given the profile of a refugee protection claimant, it is my opinion that the documentary evidence regarding the treatment of the Banyamulenge is insufficient to find that the claimant runs serious risk of persecution in the event of his return to Rwanda; his testimony established that his family does not have any particular problems as a result of this fact.

I consider these elements sufficient to find that the refugee protection claimant has not established the alleged facts on the balance of the evidence and, therefore, has not established neither a serious possibility of persecution nor that it is likely that his life would be at risk should he return.

For these reasons, having listened to the recording of the hearing, reviewed all the evidence and considered the arguments filed on appeal, I confirm the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
